prompt.context: Your client is an Australia-based PE firm that wants to acquire StarBus Australia, the biggest bus manufacturer in Australia. The client has approached you, a Consultant, to assess the transaction. In the end, you should be able to advise the client whether this is a good investment.
prompt.question: What factors will you consider first?

clarifying_info.a: StarBus sells its buses directly to both public and private schools throughout Australia; schools are the only customers.
StarBus manufactures only one type of bus that has a 10-year life cycle.

clarifying_info.q: Is the transaction fairly priced? Does the client have the financial resources to fund it?
clarifying_info.a: Assume the transaction is fairly priced and financing is not an issue for the client.

exhibits.title: Market Share Analysis
exhibits.shows: Two pie charts showing the percentage of AU school bus market share by revenue and by units sold among StarBus, MelBus/MelbourneBus, and SydBus/SydneyBus

exhibits.title: Margins Analysis
exhibits.shows: A table comparing gross margin and operating margin for StarBus, MelBus, and SydBus

framework: Market Attractiveness: Estimate market size (number of buses schools purchase per year); assess market growth over the next 3-5 years
Competition Landscape: Analyze market shares of StarBus and competitors; compare prices and margins; assess product similarity and customer overlap
Transaction: Evaluate whether the transaction is fairly priced and meets required IRR; assess whether the client has financial resources; identify synergies with portfolio companies

questions.prompt: Estimate the size of the school bus market in Australia (number of buses purchased per year).
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a bottom-up estimate segmenting school-age population by age group, applying bus-usage rates, dividing by bus capacity to get buses needed per day, then dividing by useful life. Strong candidates justify assumptions, arrive close to 640,000 buses/year, link the number to market attractiveness, and drive the case forward.

math.setup: Australian population = 25M; average life expectancy = 80 years (population distributed evenly by age); students aged 7-18 attend school; bus capacity = 50 students; bus useful life = 10 years; 200 school days/year. Bus-taking rates: ages 7-12 = 60%, ages 13-15 = 30%, ages 16-18 = 20%.
steps: Ages 7-12 (6 years): 25M x (6/80) x 60% = 25M x 0.075 x 0.6 = 1,125,000 students taking buses per day
Ages 13-15 (3 years): 25M x (3/80) x 30% = 25M x 0.0375 x 0.3 = 281,250 students taking buses per day
Ages 16-18 (3 years): 25M x (3/80) x 20% = 25M x 0.0375 x 0.2 = 187,500 students taking buses per day
Total students taking buses per day = 1,125,000 + 281,250 + 187,500 = 1,593,750
Buses required per year = 31,875 buses x 200 school days / 10-year life = 637,500 ≈ 640,000 buses per year

questions.prompt: What can cause the high market growth rate (5% actual vs 2% population growth)?
questions.guidance: This is a brainstorming question. A good candidate notices the anomaly (5% vs 2%) and questions the cause. A great candidate proactively deduces the growth is unsustainable. The key insight: 3 years ago the Australian government introduced a safety regulation requiring all schools to gradually replace old buses with new buses within 3 years. This one-time demand surge will end, and the market will likely decline over the next 5-7 years. Conclusion: market is not attractive.

questions.prompt: What do you make of Exhibit 1 (market share by revenue vs. by units)?
questions.guidance: StarBus has 40% revenue share but only 30% unit share. Competitors MelbourneBus and SydneyBus collectively have 60% in units but only 60% in revenue. This implies StarBus charges a higher price per bus than its competitors. Candidates should question why StarBus can command a price premium on a commoditized product, and drive toward cost/margin analysis.

questions.prompt: What do you make of Exhibit 2 (margins analysis)?
questions.guidance: StarBus gross margin (30%) is 10 percentage points lower than both MelBus and SydBus (40% each). Operating margins follow the same gap (10% vs 20%). Since operating efficiency (SG&A spread) is the same, the lower gross margin is driven entirely by higher COGS. Candidates should not rush to a negative conclusion; they should explore whether the higher COGS can be fixed, since an addressable problem represents turnaround potential for a PE client.

questions.prompt: Drill into the root cause of StarBus's higher COGS. Can it be fixed?
questions.guidance: Structure the COGS problem into direct material, direct labour, and overheads. The root cause path is: Higher COGS -> higher direct material cost -> same suppliers as competitors but charged at higher prices -> suppliers' industry is highly consolidated and switching costs are very high -> StarBus cannot easily renegotiate or switch suppliers. This structural disadvantage cannot be resolved quickly, making the turnaround thesis weak. A great candidate drives to this conclusion independently with minimal prompting and links it back to the investment thesis.

brainstorming.prompt: What can cause the high market growth rate of 5% when population only grows at 2%?

categories.name: Regulation / Policy changes
ideas: New government safety regulation requiring all schools to replace old buses with new buses within 3 years (actual cause)
Changes to school bus safety standards raising mandatory replacement frequency

categories.name: Demand-side factors
ideas: Increase in school enrolments above population growth rate
Expansion of school bus coverage to previously unserved areas
New private schools entering the market and purchasing fleets

categories.name: Supply-side factors
ideas: Aggressive pricing by manufacturers stimulating replacement demand
New financing options making bus purchases more accessible to schools

recommendation: Do NOT acquire StarBus Australia. The investment is not attractive for two reinforcing reasons: (1) the school bus market in Australia will decline materially over the next 3-5 years once the one-time regulatory replacement cycle ends, and (2) StarBus suffers from a structural cost disadvantage — it pays higher prices for direct materials than competitors because its suppliers operate in a highly consolidated industry with very high switching costs, meaning the margin gap cannot be closed quickly.
risks: Market decline risk: the 5% growth rate was driven by a one-off regulation; demand will revert sharply once schools have completed fleet replacement
Cost structure risk: StarBus cannot easily renegotiate supplier prices or switch suppliers given industry consolidation and high switching costs
Pricing risk: StarBus charges a premium price to offset high COGS, but in a commoditized market this premium is fragile as demand falls
next_steps: Review the valuation model — if StarBus is heavily undervalued, the acquisition could still be attractive despite adverse market and operational factors
Consider switching acquisition target to MelBus or SydBus, which have stronger margins and higher unit market shares
Assess synergies between bus manufacturers and other companies in the PE client's portfolio
